name: Extended iliofemoral approach to the acetabulum
corridor: Extensile lateral exposure created by posterior reflection of the abductors and short external rotators, with optional anterior extension into the iliac window

positioning.text: Position lateral on a radiolucent or fracture table with the entire buttock, hemipelvis, and limb accessible for manipulation and imaging.

setup.text: Prep from the posterior midline to the umbilicus and include the buttock and thigh while isolating the groin and perineum.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the posterior and anterior superior iliac spines, iliac crest, greater trochanter, and lateral femoral shaft.

incision.text: Use an inverted-J incision from the posterior iliac region along the crest to the ASIS, then continue distally over the anterolateral thigh to permit posterior flap reflection.

superficial_interval.text: Develop the separately innervated abdominal-wall–gluteal interval along the iliac crest and the sartorius–tensor fasciae latae interval anteriorly.

deep_interval.text: Elevate the gluteal flap subperiosteally from the external ilium, then release gluteus minimus, gluteus medius, piriformis, and the conjoined short external rotators with repairable tendon stumps.

layers.text: Skin and large musculocutaneous flap, fascia lata and tensor interval, subperiosteal external-iliac exposure, abductor and short-external-rotator releases, then capsule and acetabular columns.

structures_encountered.text: The approach encounters lateral femoral circumflex branches, superior gluteal neurovascular pedicle, sciatic nerve, abductors, short external rotators, rectus origins, and hip capsule.

structures_at_risk.text: The superior gluteal artery, veins, and nerve are at high risk where they exit the greater sciatic notch and travel on the deep gluteal surface.
The sciatic nerve and medial femoral circumflex artery are at risk during short-external-rotator release, notch retraction, and posterior exposure.

danger_zones.text: Continuously assess gluteal-pedicle perfusion during posterior flap retraction; pedicle thrombosis can cause catastrophic flap necrosis.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid aggressive or prolonged gluteal and sciatic-nerve retraction and protect neurovascular structures crossing the greater sciatic notch throughout reduction and fixation.

exposure.text: Exposes nearly the entire lateral innominate bone and posterior acetabulum, with anterior extension into the internal iliac fossa when required.

limitations.text: This highly morbid exposure demands complex flap mobilization and reconstruction and should be reserved for reductions not achievable safely through less-extensile approaches.

extensions.text: Extend anteriorly into the first ilioinguinal window for internal iliac-fossa access; a trochanteric osteotomy can preserve abductor insertions as a mobilized osseous fragment.

indications.text: A salvage extensile option for complex acetabular fracture patterns whose columns, dome, or chronic displacement cannot be reduced through standard anterior or posterior exposures.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid when a less-extensile approach can achieve reduction or when soft-tissue condition, vascular disease, or inability to tolerate prolonged surgery makes the flap risk unacceptable.

implant_implications.text: The broad exposure allows multiplanar column fixation, but implants and retractors must not compromise the superior gluteal pedicle, sciatic nerve, or femoral-head blood supply.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use a radiolucent setup that preserves AP and Judet views despite lateral positioning and the large reflected flap.

closure.text: Perform anatomic, mechanically secure repair of capsule, short external rotators, gluteus medius and minimus, rectus origin, iliac-crest muscle origins, fascia, and superficial layers.

complications.text: Major complications include superior-gluteal hemorrhage or thrombosis, gluteal-flap necrosis, sciatic or superior-gluteal neuropathy, abductor failure, heterotopic ossification, infection, and wound breakdown.

bailouts.text: For uncontrolled superior-gluteal bleeding, pack the notch and obtain definitive vascular control or angiographic embolization; do not pursue blind clamping into the pelvis.

procedure_applications.condition: A complex pattern cannot be reduced through a less-extensile posterior exposure
Combined lateral and anterior innominate-bone exposure is required

questions.question: Which vascular pedicle determines viability of the reflected gluteal flap?
questions.answer: The superior gluteal artery and accompanying veins.

questions.question: Why is aggressive gluteal-flap retraction dangerous?
questions.answer: It can obstruct or thrombose the superior gluteal pedicle, causing flap necrosis, and can injure the superior gluteal nerve.
